summary: Explains how multicast routing protocols interact with IGMPv3 and MLDv2, which carry source information as well as group membership. Routing protocols must manage and use that source filtering information, and this document describes how. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When people tell a TV service which shows and which senders they want, the service must remember it. This describes how routers use that extra detail.

questions: how do igmpv3 and mldv2 affect multicast routing
how do routers handle multicast source filtering
subtitle: How multicast routers use source filtering from group management protocols.

tldr.problem: IGMPv3 and MLDv2 introduce source filtering to group management, allowing hosts to specify which sources they want to receive from. Multicast routing protocols must understand and act on this source information, but the original routing protocols were not designed with this capability.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5186 specifies how multicast routing protocols (DVMRP, MOSPF, PIM-DM, PIM-SM) interpret and utilize source filter state from IGMPv3/MLDv2 reports to build forwarding trees that respect source and group membership preferences.
tldr.outcome: Multicast routing protocols can now efficiently forward only to subscribers who actually want to receive from specific sources, rather than assuming all subscribers want all sources for a group.

facts.label: Group management protocols
facts.value: IGMPv3 for IPv4, MLDv2 for IPv6

today: RFC 5186 remains Informational and describes how multicast routing protocols interact with source-filtering group management as of 2008. It has not been obsoleted and continues to be the reference for protocol interactions with IGMPv3 and MLDv2.

sections.title: Source Filtering in Multicast Group Management
sections.content:
Older multicast group management protocols like IGMPv2 and MLDv1 allowed hosts to simply join or leave a multicast group without specifying which sources they wanted to receive from. A host joining group 224.0.0.5 would receive traffic from any source sending to that group.

IGMPv3 (Internet Group Management Protocol Version 3) and MLDv2 (Multicast Listener Discovery Version 2) add source filtering capability. Hosts can now express interest in receiving traffic only from specific sources, or explicitly exclude specific sources. This creates a new requirement: multicast routing protocols must understand and act on this source information to build correct forwarding trees.

RFC 5186 describes how the major multicast routing protocols—DVMRP, MOSPF, PIM-DM, and PIM-SM—must be modified to interpret and utilize this source filtering state from IGMPv3 and MLDv2 reports.
sections.plainLanguage: Old group management said 'I want to watch group X' without saying which station. New versions let you say 'I want shows from this station' or 'I want everything except this station.' Routers need rules for using this information.

sections.title: Multicast Forwarding States with Source Filtering
sections.content:
The group management database that multicast routers use now maintains four record types instead of one. Only one record type may exist per interface and per multicast group:

EXCLUDE <> (empty exclude list) indicates interest in all sources for a group—equivalent to the single record type in older protocols. INCLUDE <> (empty include list) indicates no interest in any sources for that group. EXCLUDE <list> indicates interest in all sources except those specifically listed. INCLUDE <list> indicates interest in only the specifically listed sources.

When building forwarding state, the routing protocol examines the source address in an arriving multicast packet. If the source is in an INCLUDE list for that group on an interface, or is not listed in an EXCLUDE list, the interface is added to the downstream interfaces for that packet. Otherwise it is not added based on local group membership. This allows routers to prune traffic from sources no local subscriber wants, improving efficiency.
sections.plainLanguage: The router keeps track of four types of subscriber preferences: 'I want everything,' 'I want nothing,' 'I want everything except these sources,' and 'I want only these sources.' When a packet arrives, the router checks the source address against these lists to decide where to send it.

sections.title: DVMRP, MOSPF, and PIM-DM Protocol Interactions
sections.content:
DVMRP (Distance Vector Multicast Routing Protocol) does not inherently incorporate knowledge of multicast group sources, so it acts only on the multicast group address in IGMPv3 or MLDv2 reports, not the source filtering information. Future standardized versions of DVMRP that include pruning and grafting behaviors can follow PIM-DM rules.

MOSPF (Multicast Extensions to OSPF) uses source filter information only for building forwarding state, not for modifying its link-state flooding of group membership information.

PIM-DM (Protocol Independent Multicast - Dense Mode) uses source information in two key areas: Prune messages are sent when there are no subscribers interested in a source-group pair (when source S is in EXCLUDE state for group G, or all interest in G is terminated). Graft messages override a prune when the source filter state changes, such as when source S changes to INCLUDE state for group G after previously being pruned.
sections.plainLanguage: Different routing protocols handle the source information differently. Some ignore it, some use it just for forwarding decisions, and others use it to actively prune off branches of the tree where nobody wants a particular source. When interest changes, they send 'graft' messages to restore a pruned branch.

sections.title: PIM-SM Protocol Behavior with Source Filtering
sections.content:
PIM-SM (Protocol Independent Multicast - Sparse Mode) provides the most sophisticated source filtering integration. PIM-SM routers interpret IGMPv3/MLDv2 messages differently based on whether the addressed group is in the Any Source Multicast (ASM) range or the Source Specific Multicast (SSM) range.

In ASM mode, when a PIM-SM router receives an IGMPv3/MLDv2 report with a zero-length EXCLUDE list (indicating 'I want everything'), it sends a (*,G) join towards the rendezvous point. When the report affects source information, the router sends an (S,G) join towards the specific source, optimizing the join process and facilitating SSM adoption. The router sending a (*,G) join is responsible for filtering data according to the IGMPv3 database before forwarding.

For prunes, when IGMPv3/MLDv2 shows no interest in a specific source-group pair or when all interest in a group times out, the router sends (S,G) prunes upstream or (S,G) and (*,G) prunes to stop all flow.

PIM-SSM (Source Specific Multicast) behavior with IGMPv3/MLDv2 is defined separately in the PIM-SM specification and operates on SSM-range groups where source information is essential.
sections.plainLanguage: PIM-SM is the most flexible: it sends different join messages depending on what subscribers want. If they want all sources, it joins toward a central point. If they want specific sources, it joins directly to those sources. When interest drops, it sends prune messages to stop the flow.
